title: How To Catch A Cheater With Math
beats: Blob coin-flip game; rumor of trick coins that land heads more than half the time
Five flips each, results from 0 to 5 heads; who would you accuse?
Five of five heads was a cheater only 88% of the time in the earlier game; certainty is impossible; names frequentist hypothesis testing
Three goals for the test: few false accusations, catch cheaters, few flips; pause to try your own
One flip at a time: heads, heads, heads; each step halves the chance an innocent looks this way
Multiply probabilities only if independent; zero false accusation is unreachable
Pick the standard 5% threshold; five heads in a row is 1 in 32
1000 players, half cheaters; predict, then four categories; goal one met, few cheaters caught
Positive, negative, true, false terms after the concept; admits false positive rate wording is confusing and keeps plain language
Goal two needs a number: 80% power; cheater coin 75% heads is an assumption, called effect size
0.75 to the fifth is about 24%, matches the trial
Need a mixed-heads rule; two- and three-flip distributions grow into bar graphs
Binomial distribution named and deferred to a later video
Threshold line on two bar graphs maps to four categories; shifting threshold trades goals
Overlap means five flips cannot do both; 100 flips separates but breaks goal three
Computer search: 23 flips, accuse at 16 or more heads
Test two blobs (17 and 13 heads); p-value introduced as a per-result false positive rate, 'kind of'
Trade-offs: 1% false accusation gives 47% power; 99% and 1% needs 80 flips; two goals fixed limit the third
Mystery group: only a quarter caught; real cheaters used 60%, not 75%; assumption was wrong
Right design for 60% needs 158 flips and 90 heads; people forget assumptions are assumptions
Framework: yes/no question, models for each answer, test that separates them; dominant in real science

metrics.misconception: yes: treating an assumed effect size as fact (staged trap at 18:54); also mix-up of false positive rate denominator at 7:30
metrics.brute_force: yes 2:33: flip by flip, accuse after one, two, three heads, probability halving
metrics.examples: flip counts grow 1 to 5 to 10 to 23 to 158; 1000-blob groups three times, third with hidden truth
metrics.ending: Staged failure of the 75% assumption, then framework summary and Bayesian teaser

new_moves.name: staged-assumption-trap
new_moves.what: Sets up a prediction, hides the truth, lets the viewer be wrong because of an earlier stated assumption, then says it was deliberate

new_moves.name: label-every-choice
new_moves.what: Repeatedly flags whether a number is a choice or an assumption

new_moves.name: vocabulary-with-warning
new_moves.what: Introduces jargon, admits which term is confusing and keeps plain wording

new_moves.name: meta-prediction-prompt
new_moves.what: Tells the viewer prediction prompts are becoming rote and hints this one will go wrong

theory: Statistics is taught as designing a test against three explicit goals, so every number (5%, 80%, 75%, 23 flips) is something the viewer chose or assumed rather than received. The capstone staged failure teaches that assumptions silently become facts by letting the viewer fall into it.
velocity: Orchestrator: define goals first and let the learner design the test before showing the standard answer
Learner model: tag each number as a choice or an assumption and quiz recall of assumptions before a prediction
Scene builder: bar-graph pair with a draggable threshold that updates the four category counts live
Voice: delay jargon until a concept is felt, and warn when a term has a tricky denominator
Evals: check for a deliberate failure case that exposes a stated assumption
quote: It's very easy to forget that assumptions are assumptions
